claim: Starvation causes a drop in intracellular pH in budding yeast.
source: In budding yeast, starvation causes a drop in intracellular pH, but the functional role of this pH change is not well understood.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact.

claim: The enzyme glutamine synthetase (Gln1) forms filaments at low pH.
source: Here, we show that the enzyme glutamine synthetase (Gln1) forms filaments at low pH and that filament formation leads to enzymatic inactivation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Filament formation by Gln1 leads to enzymatic inactivation.
source: Here, we show that the enzyme glutamine synthetase (Gln1) forms filaments at low pH and that filament formation leads to enzymatic inactivation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: Filament formation by Gln1 is a highly cooperative process.
source: Filament formation by Gln1 is a highly cooperative process, strongly dependent on macromolecular crowding, and involves back-to-back stacking of cylindrical homo-decamers into filaments that associate laterally to form higher order fibrils.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental observations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Filament formation by Gln1 is strongly dependent on macromolecular crowding.
source: Filament formation by Gln1 is a highly cooperative process, strongly dependent on macromolecular crowding, and involves back-to-back stacking of cylindrical homo-decamers into filaments that associate laterally to form higher order fibrils.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3.

claim: Gln1 filament formation involves back-to-back stacking of cylindrical homo-decamers.
source: Filament formation by Gln1 is a highly cooperative process, strongly dependent on macromolecular crowding, and involves back-to-back stacking of cylindrical homo-decamers into filaments that associate laterally to form higher order fibrils.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural analysis and mutagenesis data in Figure 2.

claim: Gln1 filaments associate laterally to form higher order fibrils.
source: Filament formation by Gln1 is a highly cooperative process, strongly dependent on macromolecular crowding, and involves back-to-back stacking of cylindrical homo-decamers into filaments that associate laterally to form higher order fibrils.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 2D.

claim: Other metabolic enzymes also assemble into filaments at low pH.
source: Other metabolic enzymes also assemble into filaments at low pH.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated experimentally in Figure 5.

claim: Filament formation is a general mechanism to inactivate and store key metabolic enzymes during a state of advanced cellular starvation.
source: Hence, we propose that filament formation is a general mechanism to inactivate and store key metabolic enzymes during a state of advanced cellular starvation.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Eukaryotes have achieved organizational complexity by restricting specific biochemical reactions to membrane-bound organelles.
source: Eukaryotes in particular have achieved a high level of organizational complexity by restricting specific biochemical reactions to membrane-bound organelles in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Phase-separated macromolecular assemblies provide a strategy for localized biochemistry.
source: A different but equally effective strategy for localized biochemistry involves the formation of phase-separated macromolecular assemblies, which are built de novo from proteins and RNAs (Brangwynne, 2011; Hyman and Simons, 2012; O'Connell et al., 2012; Wilson and Gitai, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mesoscale assemblies can be categorized into liquid-like and crystalline groups based on their physicochemical properties.
source: Based on their physicochemical properties they can be categorized into two distinct groups: liquid-like and crystalline.
evidence: This is stated as a classification scheme in the introduction.

claim: Liquid-like assemblies are disordered and very dynamic with components turning over on the order of seconds to minutes.
source: Liquid-like assemblies are disordered and very dynamic (the components turn over on the order of seconds to minutes) (Brangwynne et al., 2009, 2011; Li et al., 2012), whereas crystalline assemblies are more ordered and static (Yeates et al., 2010; Wilson and Gitai, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Crystalline assemblies are more ordered and static than liquid-like assemblies.
source: Liquid-like assemblies are disordered and very dynamic (the components turn over on the order of seconds to minutes) (Brangwynne et al., 2009, 2011; Li et al., 2012), whereas crystalline assemblies are more ordered and static (Yeates et al., 2010; Wilson and Gitai, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Metabolic enzymes are able to self-assemble into higher order structures.
source: Metabolic enzymes in particular are able to self-assemble into higher order structures (O'Connell et al., 2012), suggesting an important role in regulating the metabolism of cells.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Paul Srere and colleagues proposed that metabolic enzymes undergo static and dynamic interactions to spatiotemporally organize and regulate metabolic pathways.
source: These findings establish a link to earlier work from Paul Srere and colleagues, who proposed that metabolic enzymes undergo static and dynamic interactions to spatiotemporally organize and regulate metabolic pathways (Srere, 1987).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Cytidine triphosphate synthase forms cytoskeletal filaments with cell morphological functions in bacteria.
source: A particularly striking example is that of cytidine triphosphate synthase, a bacterial enzyme that forms cytoskeletal filaments with cell morphological functions (Ingerson-Mahar et al., 2010; Barry and Gitai, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Large-scale studies in budding yeast identified several metabolic enzymes that form punctate or filamentous structures in the cytoplasm.
source: Recent large-scale studies in budding yeast identified several metabolic enzymes that form punctate or filamentous structures in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as background information.

claim: Cytidine triphosphate synthase is an enzyme involved in the synthesis of cytosine nucleotides that forms structures in yeast.
source: Examples include cytidine triphosphate synthase (Noree et al., 2010), an enzyme involved in the synthesis of cytosine nucleotides, and glutamine synthetase (Narayanaswamy et al., 2009), an enzyme that promotes the conversion of glutamate into glutamine.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Glutamine synthetase is an enzyme that promotes the conversion of glutamate into glutamine.
source: Examples include cytidine triphosphate synthase (Noree et al., 2010), an enzyme involved in the synthesis of cytosine nucleotides, and glutamine synthetase (Narayanaswamy et al., 2009), an enzyme that promotes the conversion of glutamate into glutamine.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Filament formation by metabolic enzymes was most frequently observed when cells entered stationary phase or were depleted of glucose.
source: The metabolic reactions catalyzed by these newly identified enzymes were diverse, but the conditions under which they assembled appeared to be similar: filament formation was most frequently observed, when cells entered stationary phase or were depleted of their primary energy source: glucose.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an observation from previous studies.

claim: GFP-tagged Gln1 was evenly distributed in dividing cells but coalesced into fluorescent foci in cells maintained in phosphate buffer.
source: In agreement with previous studies (Narayanaswamy et al., 2009), we found that GFP-tagged Gln1 was evenly distributed in dividing cells but coalesced into fluorescent foci in cells that were maintained in a phosphate buffer (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Some Gln1 foci displayed a rod-like shape, suggesting filamentous structures.
source: While most of these foci had a punctate appearance, we noticed a few that displayed a rod-like shape. This suggested that Gln1 might be able to assemble into filamentous structures, but at the same time it implied that the efficiency of filament formation was very low.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an observation from microscopy experiments.

claim: The homo-oligomeric structure of Gln1 allows mixed oligomers composed of tagged and untagged monomers.
source: To exclude a potential interference from the GFP tag, we made use of the fact that the homo-oligomeric structure of Gln1 allows mixed oligomers composed of tagged and untagged monomers.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a property of Gln1 used in the experimental design.

claim: Co-expression of untagged and GFP-tagged Gln1 resulted in assembly into filaments.
source: Indeed, when we co-expressed untagged and GFP-tagged Gln1 in yeast, the punctate localization pattern disappeared, and Gln1-GFP assembled into a few filaments per cell (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: FlAsH-labeled Gln1 assembled into filaments in cells transferred from media to buffer.
source: Indeed, FlAsH-labeled Gln1 assembled into filaments in cells that were transferred from media to buffer (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: mCherry-tagged Gln1 assembled into filaments.
source: Indeed, unlike GFP-tagged Gln1, mCherry-tagged Gln1 assembled into filaments (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 1A.

claim: mCherry is compatible with the filamentous state of Gln1.
source: These data indicate that mCherry is compatible with the filamentous state and therefore a suitable fluorophore to study the localization of Gln1 in living cells.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental observations with mCherry-tagged Gln1.

claim: mCherry-tagged Gln1 was diffusely localized in dividing cells but formed filaments when the growth medium lacked a carbon source.
source: Using live cell microscopy, we found that mCherry-tagged Gln1 was diffusely localized in dividing cells but formed filaments when the growth medium lacked a carbon source (33% of the cells had filaments after 4 hr of glucose starvation) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 1B.

claim: 33% of cells had filaments after 4 hours of glucose starvation.
source: Using live cell microscopy, we found that mCherry-tagged Gln1 was diffusely localized in dividing cells but formed filaments when the growth medium lacked a carbon source (33% of the cells had filaments after 4 hr of glucose starvation) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 1B.

claim: When cells were transferred into a phosphate buffer with no metabolizable nutrients, filaments were detectable in all cells.
source: Importantly, when we transferred the cells into a phosphate buffer that contained no metabolizable nutrients, filaments were detectable in all cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 1C.

claim: Under conditions of severe starvation, the filament formation phenotype becomes fully penetrant.
source: Thus, under conditions of severe starvation, the filament formation phenotype becomes fully penetrant.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the observation that all cells form filaments in phosphate buffer.

claim: Filament formation by metabolic enzymes is a starvation-induced cellular adaptation.
source: This suggests that filament formation by metabolic enzymes is a starvation-induced cellular adaptation.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: On average, filament assembly started 50 minutes after onset of advanced starvation conditions.
source: On average, filament assembly started 50 min (n = 179; SD = 43.9 min) after onset of advanced starvation conditions (Figure 1D and Video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by time-lapse microscopy data in Figure 1D and Video 1.

claim: There is extensive cell-to-cell variation in the timing of filament assembly.
source: However, we observed extensive variation from cell to cell, suggesting that yeast vary in their ability to deal with sudden energy depletion (Video 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by time-lapse microscopy data in Video 2.

claim: Addition of glucose to buffer was sufficient to prevent filament formation.
source: Importantly, addition of glucose to buffer was sufficient to prevent filament formation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 1C.

claim: Cells can fully recover from the state of advanced starvation.
source: We also found that cells can fully recover from the state of advanced starvation.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on observations of filament dissolution and cell cycle re-entry.

claim: Upon resupply of nutrients, filaments dissolved very rapidly, and shortly after filament dissolution cells re-entered into the cell cycle.
source: Upon resupply of nutrients, filament dissolved very rapidly, and shortly after filament dissolution cells re-entered into the cell cycle (Figure 1E, Videos 3 and 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by time-lapse microscopy data in Figure 1E and Videos 3 and 4.

claim: On average, filament dissolution was completed approximately 18 minutes after nutrient addition.
source: On average, filament dissolution was completed ∼18 min after nutrient addition (n = 65; SD = 11.6 min).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on time-lapse microscopy measurements.

claim: Gln1 dynamically and reversibly assembles into filaments when yeast cells are exposed to conditions of advanced starvation.
source: We conclude that Gln1 dynamically and reversibly assembles into filaments when yeast cells are exposed to conditions of advanced starvation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experimental observations of filament formation and dissolution.

claim: A recent study reported a high-resolution crystal structure for yeast Gln1.
source: A recent study reported a high-resolution crystal structure for yeast Gln1 (He et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Yeast Gln1 is composed of two pentameric rings that interact to form a face-to-face homo-decamer.
source: The enzyme is composed of two pentameric rings that interact to form a face-to-face homo-decamer.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the crystal structure from He et al., 2009.

claim: The structural arrangement of yeast Gln1 is identical to those of mammalian and plant glutamine synthetases.
source: This structural arrangement is identical to those of mammalian and plant glutamine synthetases.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a comparison to other glutamine synthetases.

claim: The crystal structure of yeast Gln1 revealed a new back-to-back association between two decamers.
source: Curiously, however, the crystal structure of yeast Gln1 also revealed a new back-to-back association between two decamers (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Three mutations (E186K, P83R, T49E) abrogated the ability of Gln1 to form filaments in starved cells.
source: We found three mutations (E186K, P83R, T49E) that abrogated the ability of Gln1 to form filaments in starved cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 2B.

claim: The Y81A mutant had a slightly increased propensity to form filaments.
source: The Y81A mutant had a slightly increased propensity to form filaments, whereas the R23E mutant formed filaments constitutively, regardless of the growth conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on microscopy observations.

claim: The R23E mutant formed filaments constitutively, regardless of the growth conditions.
source: The Y81A mutant had a slightly increased propensity to form filaments, whereas the R23E mutant formed filaments constitutively, regardless of the growth conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 2B.

claim: The double mutant (R23E, T49E) was no longer able to form filaments.
source: Indeed, the double mutant (R23E, T49E) was no longer able to form filaments (Figure 2B), indicating that the increased propensity to form filaments can be overcome by an inhibitory second site mutation.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 2B.

claim: The increased propensity to form filaments can be overcome by an inhibitory second site mutation.
source: Indeed, the double mutant (R23E, T49E) was no longer able to form filaments (Figure 2B), indicating that the increased propensity to form filaments can be overcome by an inhibitory second site mutation.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the double mutant data.

claim: The propensity to form filaments can be modulated by specific mutations in Gln1.
source: These findings indicate that the propensity to form filaments can be modulated by specific mutations in Gln1.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the mutagenesis experiments.

claim: The decamer–decamer interface is biologically important.
source: They also suggest that the decamer–decamer interface is biologically important.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the mutagenesis results.

claim: The predominant form of Gln1 is a decamer.
source: As can be seen in Figure 2C, the predominant form of Gln1 was a decamer.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by blue native PAGE data in Figure 2C.

claim: Higher molecular weight forms of Gln1 were predominantly detectable for the wild-type and the R23E variant.
source: Importantly, however, we also identified distinct bands that corresponded to higher molecular weight forms of the enzyme. These assemblies were predominantly detectable for the wild-type and the R23E variant.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by blue native PAGE data in Figure 2C.

claim: The R23E variant showed an increased number of higher order assemblies compared to wild-type Gln1.
source: Moreover, when compared to wild-type Gln1, the constitutively filament-forming R23E variant showed an increased number of these higher order assemblies.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by blue native PAGE data in Figure 2C.

claim: Gln1 filaments could not be stained with Thioflavin T.
source: As can be seen in Figure 2—figure supplements 4 and 5, we could not find evidence for cross-β structure.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by Thioflavin T staining data in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Gln1 filaments are not resistant to detergent in semi-denaturing detergent–agarose gel electrophoresis.
source: As can be seen in Figure 2—figure supplements 4 and 5, we could not find evidence for cross-β structure.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by SDD-AGE data in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Gln1 retains a near-native structure when it assembles into filaments.
source: Thus, we conclude that Gln1 retains a near-native structure when it assembles into filaments.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the lack of cross-β structure and electron microscopy observations.

claim: Electron micrographs of R23E Gln1 show a large number of filaments which are laterally aligned into higher order bundles.
source: The ultrastructural features of the mCherry-positive structures are shown in Figure 2D. The electron micrographs show a large number of filaments, which are laterally aligned into higher order bundles.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by CLEM data in Figure 2D.

claim: The side-by-side bundling of Gln1 filaments is consistent with the growth pattern of the filaments.
source: This side-by-side bundling is consistent with the growth pattern of the filaments, which was predominately in the longitudinal direction but also included some increase in circumference over time (see Video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results as a correlation between electron microscopy and time-lapse microscopy observations.

claim: Fibrillar structures were identified in the cytoplasm of R23E-expressing cells but not in control cells.
source: Indeed, we could also identify fibrillar structures in the cytoplasm of R23E-expressing cells but not in control cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: The mCherry tag has some influence on the packing density of Gln1 filaments.
source: However, we noticed that the filaments were in closer contact, suggesting that the mCherry tag has some influence on the packing density.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from comparing mCherry-tagged and untagged R23E filaments.

claim: Gln1 assembles into filaments by a back-to-back stacking mechanism.
source: Together, these findings indicate that Gln1 assembles into filaments by a back-to-back stacking mechanism.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the structural and mutagenesis data.

claim: Once formed, Gln1 filaments can organize into higher order fibrils.
source: Once formed, these filaments can organize into higher order fibrils.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the electron microscopy observations.

claim: R23E Gln1 had a strongly increased propensity to assemble into higher order forms compared to wild-type and E186K.
source: As can be seen in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, R23E Gln1 had a strongly increased propensity to assemble into higher order forms. This propensity was reduced in wild-type Gln1 and absent from a variant that had lost the ability to assemble into filaments in yeast cells (E186K).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by dynamic light scattering and gel exclusion chromatography data in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Purified R23E Gln1 particles were organized into chains.
source: Our analysis revealed abundant cylindrical particles, consistent with the reported structure of Gln1 (He et al., 2009). Interestingly, these particles were organized into chains, providing further support for the proposed back-to-back assembly mechanism.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by electron microscopy data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Higher order structures resembling fibrillar structures in yeast were not identified in purified R23E Gln1.
source: However, we were unable to identify higher order structures that resembled previously observed fibrillar structures in yeast, suggesting that an important factor was missing.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an observation from electron microscopy of purified protein.

claim: When yeast cells containing Gln1 filaments were lysed, the filaments were unstable.
source: When we lysed filament-containing yeast, the filaments were unstable (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 3B.

claim: When Ficoll 70 was added to the lysis buffer at a concentration close to the physiological concentration of macromolecules, the filaments remained intact.
source: Strikingly, when we added the crowding agent Ficoll 70 at a concentration close to the physiological concentration of macromolecules (200 mg/ml), the filaments remained intact (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 3C.

claim: R23E Gln1 formed filamentous structures in the presence of a crowder but not in its absence.
source: Intriguingly, we found that R23E Gln1 formed filamentous structures in the presence of a crowder but not in its absence (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by in vitro reconstitution data in Figure 3D.

claim: The assembly-incompetent variant P83R did not form structures in the presence of a crowder.
source: Importantly, similar structures could not be detected when we replaced R23E with the assembly-incompetent variant P83R.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a control experiment for the in vitro reconstitution.

claim: In vitro reconstituted Gln1 filaments are able to assemble into higher order bundles.
source: Further inspection of in vitro formed Gln1 filaments revealed structures of varying thickness (Figure 3—figure supplement 3). This suggests that in vitro reconstituted filaments are able to assemble into higher order bundles, as in yeast cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The assembly of Gln1 is strongly dependent on macromolecular crowding but independent of other cellular components.
source: Thus, we conclude that the assembly of Gln1 is strongly dependent on macromolecular crowding but independent of other cellular components.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the in vitro reconstitution experiments.

claim: The stability of R23E filaments could be increased by acidifying the lysis buffer.
source: Again experiments with lysates of R23E-expressing cells were revealing. These experiments showed that the stability of R23E filaments could not only be increased by crowders but also by acidifying the lysis buffer.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on experiments with lysates at different pH values.

claim: A cell lysate prepared with a lysis buffer of pH 5 contained abundant filaments.
source: A cell lysate prepared with a lysis buffer of pH 5 contained abundant filaments, while the filaments began to fall apart when the lysis buffer was adjusted to pH 6, and they were absent from lysates adjusted to pH 7 or 8 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 4A.

claim: Filaments began to fall apart when the lysis buffer was adjusted to pH 6.
source: A cell lysate prepared with a lysis buffer of pH 5 contained abundant filaments, while the filaments began to fall apart when the lysis buffer was adjusted to pH 6, and they were absent from lysates adjusted to pH 7 or 8 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 4A.

claim: Filaments were absent from lysates adjusted to pH 7 or 8.
source: A cell lysate prepared with a lysis buffer of pH 5 contained abundant filaments, while the filaments began to fall apart when the lysis buffer was adjusted to pH 6, and they were absent from lysates adjusted to pH 7 or 8 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 4A.

claim: The intracellular pH of yeast cells drops significantly when yeast are depleted of glucose.
source: The intracellular pH of yeast cells drops significantly when yeast are depleted of their primary energy source glucose (Orij et al., 2009; Dechant et al., 2010; Orij et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Yeast cells have to continuously expend energy to maintain the proton gradient across the plasma membrane.
source: This is because yeast cells have to continuously expend energy to maintain the proton gradient across the plasma membrane (usually yeast media are acidic).
evidence: This is stated in the results as an explanation for pH changes during starvation.

claim: Acidified yeast abundantly formed filamentous structures, despite the presence of glucose.
source: Strikingly, acidified yeast abundantly formed filamentous structures, despite the presence of glucose (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 4B.

claim: Starved yeast maintained in a buffer of pH 7 contained shorter and smaller filaments than yeast in a buffer of pH 5.
source: Indeed, starved yeast maintained in a buffer of pH 7 contained shorter and smaller filaments than yeast in a buffer of pH 5 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 4C.

claim: Filaments were largely absent when the buffer was adjusted to pH 8.
source: Moreover, filaments were largely absent when the buffer was adjusted to pH 8.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on microscopy observations.

claim: Gln1 formed filamentous structures in an acidic buffer but not in a control buffer with a basic pH.
source: Indeed, Gln1 formed filamentous structures in the acidic buffer but not in the control buffer with a basic pH (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by in vitro reconstitution data in Figure 4D.

claim: The assembly-deficient variant P83R did not assemble into higher order structures in an acidic buffer.
source: Importantly, this effect was specific, because the assembly-deficient variant P83R did not assemble into higher order structures in an acidic buffer.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a control experiment for pH-induced assembly.

claim: Gln1 progressively assembled into higher order structures when exposed to an acidic buffer.
source: As can be seen in Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Gln1 progressively assembled into higher order structures, whereas a mutant version of Gln1 (E186K) did not.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by dynamic light scattering data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: A mutant version of Gln1 (E186K) did not assemble into higher order structures when exposed to an acidic buffer.
source: As can be seen in Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Gln1 progressively assembled into higher order structures, whereas a mutant version of Gln1 (E186K) did not.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by dynamic light scattering data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Exposure to an acidic buffer did not lead to an extensive alteration of the secondary structure of Gln1.
source: Moreover, exposure to an acidic buffer did not lead to an extensive alteration of the secondary structure of Gln1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the protein retains its structural integrity under these conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by circular dichroism data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Gln1 assembly is directly regulated by protons.
source: Thus, we conclude that Gln1 assembly is directly regulated by protons and that the trigger for filament formation in yeast cells is a starvation-induced drop in the intracellular pH.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the in vitro pH experiments.

claim: The trigger for filament formation in yeast cells is a starvation-induced drop in the intracellular pH.
source: Thus, we conclude that Gln1 assembly is directly regulated by protons and that the trigger for filament formation in yeast cells is a starvation-induced drop in the intracellular pH.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the pH manipulation experiments.

claim: All three tested proteins (Ura8, Glt1, Gcn3) formed filaments in a strongly pH-dependent manner.
source: Intriguingly, we found that all three proteins formed filaments in a strongly pH-dependent manner (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 5A.

claim: Filament formation by Ura8, Glt1, and Gcn3 was almost completely abrogated at a neutral or basic pH.
source: Moreover, filament formation was almost completely abrogated at a neutral or basic pH.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on microscopy observations in Figure 5A.

claim: Cells suspended in a DNP-containing buffer of pH 5 or pH 6 showed widespread filament formation, despite the presence of glucose.
source: Indeed, cells suspended in a DNP-containing buffer of pH 5 or pH 6 showed widespread filament formation, despite the presence of glucose (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by microscopy data in Figure 5B.

claim: Filaments were absent from cells maintained in a DNP-containing buffer of pH 7.
source: However, filaments were absent from cells maintained in a DNP-containing buffer of pH 7.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on microscopy observations.

claim: pH changes are a general trigger for the formation of filaments by metabolic enzymes.
source: This indicates that pH changes are a general trigger for the formation of filaments by metabolic enzymes.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experiments with multiple enzymes.

claim: Gln1 was progressively inactivated under conditions of advanced starvation.
source: Indeed, Gln1 was progressively inactivated under conditions of advanced starvation (Figure 6A), and the extent of inactivation correlated with the amount of filament formation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by enzymatic activity assay data in Figure 6A.

claim: The extent of Gln1 inactivation correlated with the amount of filament formation.
source: Indeed, Gln1 was progressively inactivated under conditions of advanced starvation (Figure 6A), and the extent of inactivation correlated with the amount of filament formation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The R23E variant displayed a strongly reduced synthetase activity.
source: As can be seen in Figure 6B, the R23E variant displayed a strongly reduced synthetase activity.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by enzymatic activity assay data in Figure 6B.

claim: The constitutively assembling R23E variant had a strongly diminished ability to grow.
source: Consistent with the essential function of Gln1, the constitutively assembling R23E variant had a strongly diminished ability to grow (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by growth assay data in Figure 6C.

claim: The growth deficiency of R23E was abrogated by a second site mutation (T49E) that prevents filament formation.
source: Importantly, this growth deficiency was abrogated by a second site mutation that prevents filament formation (T49E), indicating that filament formation is the cause of the reduced growth rate.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by growth assay data in Figure 6C.

claim: Filament formation is the cause of the reduced growth rate in R23E cells.
source: Importantly, this growth deficiency was abrogated by a second site mutation that prevents filament formation (T49E), indicating that filament formation is the cause of the reduced growth rate.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the double mutant growth data.

claim: Cells growing on glutamine as the sole nitrogen source showed no growth defect.
source: Moreover, cells growing on glutamine as the sole nitrogen source (Figure 6—figure supplement 2) showed no growth defect, suggesting that this deficiency was due to the inability of the cells to produce sufficient amounts of the growth-promoting amino acid glutamine.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by growth assay data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The growth deficiency of R23E was due to the inability of the cells to produce sufficient amounts of glutamine.
source: Moreover, cells growing on glutamine as the sole nitrogen source (Figure 6—figure supplement 2) showed no growth defect, suggesting that this deficiency was due to the inability of the cells to produce sufficient amounts of the growth-promoting amino acid glutamine.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the growth assay data.

claim: Filament formation during advanced starvation conditions silences the enzymatic activity of Gln1.
source: Based on these findings, we conclude that filament formation during advanced starvation conditions silences the enzymatic activity of Gln1.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the activity and growth assay data.

claim: Gln1 filaments dissolve rapidly when yeast cells re-enter the cell cycle.
source: Gln1 filaments dissolve rapidly when yeast cells re-enter the cell cycle, and the disassembled enzyme complexes are fully functional.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the experimental observations.

claim: The disassembled Gln1 enzyme complexes are fully functional.
source: Gln1 filaments dissolve rapidly when yeast cells re-enter the cell cycle, and the disassembled enzyme complexes are fully functional.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the observation that cells can divide after filament dissolution.

claim: After the filaments had dissolved, the cells started to divide again.
source: Indeed, after the filaments had dissolved, the cells started to divide again (Figure 6D and Video 5).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by time-lapse microscopy data in Figure 6D and Video 5.

claim: Growth stopped after several rounds of cell division, presumably because the amount of Gln1 was diluted below a critical concentration.
source: Growth only stopped after several rounds of cell division, presumably because the amount of Gln1 was diluted below a critical concentration.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the observation that cells eventually stop dividing.

claim: Starvation-induced filaments can serve as storage depots for Gln1.
source: Thus, we conclude that starvation-induced filaments can serve as storage depots for Gln1.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the GAL promoter experiment.

claim: The Y81A strain showed significantly slower growth after exit from starvation than wild-type cells.
source: As can be seen in Figure 6E, the Y81A strain showed significantly slower growth after exit from starvation than wild-type cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by growth curve data in Figure 6E.

claim: Exit from starvation is dependent on stored enzymes.
source: Thus, we conclude that exit from starvation is dependent on stored enzymes and that the rate of filament dissolution determines the timing of re-growth.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the Y81A growth experiment.

claim: The rate of filament dissolution determines the timing of re-growth.
source: Thus, we conclude that exit from starvation is dependent on stored enzymes and that the rate of filament dissolution determines the timing of re-growth.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the Y81A growth experiment.

claim: The regrowth of yeast was severely impaired in filamentation-inhibiting buffer (pH 7 or 8).
source: As can be seen in Figure 7A, the regrowth of yeast was severely impaired in filamentation-inhibiting buffer (pH 7 or 8), whereas cells maintained in filamentation-promoting buffer (pH 6) showed fast recovery.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by growth curve data in Figure 7A.

claim: Cells maintained in filamentation-promoting buffer (pH 6) showed fast recovery.
source: As can be seen in Figure 7A, the regrowth of yeast was severely impaired in filamentation-inhibiting buffer (pH 7 or 8), whereas cells maintained in filamentation-promoting buffer (pH 6) showed fast recovery.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by growth curve data in Figure 7A.

claim: Filament formation by metabolic enzymes is required for recovery from severe starvation.
source: This suggests that filament formation by metabolic enzymes is required for recovery from severe starvation.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the pH-dependent recovery experiment.

claim: Filament formation is a specific adaptation that enables yeast to endure severe energy depletion stress.
source: Thus, we conclude that filament formation is a specific adaptation that enables yeast to endure severe energy depletion stress.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the recovery experiments.

claim: Starvation induces the self-assembly of yeast glutamine synthetase into filaments by a simple back-to-back stacking mechanism.
source: We demonstrate that starvation induces the self-assembly of yeast glutamine synthetase into filaments by a simple back-to-back stacking mechanism (see Figure 7B for a model of assembly).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: Filament formation is triggered by starvation-induced acidification of the cytosol.
source: We further show that filament formation is triggered by starvation-induced acidification of the cytosol and results in enzyme inactivation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: Filament formation results in enzyme inactivation.
source: We further show that filament formation is triggered by starvation-induced acidification of the cytosol and results in enzyme inactivation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the findings.

claim: The catalytic inactivation of Gln1 by filament formation is reversible.
source: This catalytic inactivation is reversible, arguing that filaments are temporary storage depots for Gln1.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the observation that cells can recover after filament dissolution.

claim: Other filament-forming enzymes show a strikingly similar sensitivity to pH.
source: Other filament-forming enzymes show a strikingly similar sensitivity to pH, and their growth-associated functions are probably not needed during advanced starvation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the experiments with Ura8, Glt1, and Gcn3.

claim: The formation of inactive enzyme assemblies may be a general principle which allows cells to adapt to low energy levels.
source: This suggests that the formation of inactive enzyme assemblies may be a general principle, which allows cells to adapt to low energy levels.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a proposed general principle.

claim: Filament formation regulates the regrowth of yeast after severe starvation.
source: Consistent with this, we found that filament formation regulates the regrowth of yeast after severe starvation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the recovery experiments.

claim: Quiescence-associated subcellular structures, such as proteasome storage granules and actin bodies, also form in a pH-dependent manner.
source: Recent findings indicate that quiescence-associated subcellular structures, such as proteasome storage granules and actin bodies, also form in a pH-dependent manner (Peters et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: pH changes have been implicated in the regulation of stress-induced G protein signaling.
source: Moreover, pH changes have been implicated in the regulation of stress-induced G protein signaling (Isom et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Intracellular pH changes serve as a global messenger to signal the depletion of energy during starvation and cellular quiescence.
source: This strongly reinforces the notion that intracellular pH changes serve as a global messenger to signal the depletion of energy during starvation and cellular quiescence (Dechant et al., 2010; Orij et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: pH-induced formation of filamentous structures may be a more widespread phenomenon in nature.
source: In fact, pH-induced formation of filamentous structures may be a more widespread phenomenon in nature, as shown for example by the finding that spider silk formation is induced by low pH (Kronqvist et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Spider silk formation is induced by low pH.
source: In fact, pH-induced formation of filamentous structures may be a more widespread phenomenon in nature, as shown for example by the finding that spider silk formation is induced by low pH (Kronqvist et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Gln1 has a theoretical isoelectric point of around 6.
source: We noticed that Gln1 has a theoretical isoelectric point of around 6.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an observation relevant to understanding pH effects.

claim: Starvation-induced changes in the cytosolic pH will strongly reduce the net charge of Gln1.
source: Starvation-induced changes in the cytosolic pH will therefore strongly reduce its net charge.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an inference from the isoelectric point.

claim: An overall reduction of repulsive interactions or altered charge distributions at the interface are likely to be the driving force for Gln1 assembly.
source: Thus, an overall reduction of repulsive interactions or altered charge distributions at the interface—which the mutations introduced in this study may modulate—are likely to be the driving force for assembly.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a proposed mechanism.

claim: A drop in intracellular pH induces the formation of an attractive interface at the two ends of a decameric Gln1 particle.
source: Regardless of the specific mechanism, what is evident is that a drop in intracellular pH induces the formation of an attractive interface at the two ends of a decameric Gln1 particle.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: The steric self-compatibility of the interface and the highly symmetric cylindrical structure of Gln1 promote the assembly of Gln1 into extended filaments.
source: The steric self-compatibility of this interface and the highly symmetric cylindrical structure of Gln1 then promote the assembly of Gln1 into extended filaments.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an explanation for filament formation.

claim: The individual stacking reactions of Gln1 seem to be quite stable at low pH.
source: The individual stacking reactions seem to be quite stable at low pH, whereas the final filamentous structure was vulnerable to even mild perturbations.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the experimental observations.

claim: The final filamentous structure of Gln1 was vulnerable to even mild perturbations.
source: The individual stacking reactions seem to be quite stable at low pH, whereas the final filamentous structure was vulnerable to even mild perturbations.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the experimental observations.

claim: The higher order assembly of filaments into microscopically visible fibrils is a cooperative and less favorable process.
source: This suggests that the higher order assembly of filaments into microscopically visible fibrils is a cooperative and less favorable process.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the stability observations.

claim: The formation of fibrils was strongly dependent on a macromolecular crowding agent.
source: In agreement with this, we found that the formation of fibrils was strongly dependent on a macromolecular crowding agent.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the crowding experiments.

claim: The assembly reaction is driven enthalpically by chemical interface–interface interactions and entropically by excluded volume effects.
source: This indicates that the assembly reaction is not only driven enthalpically by chemical interface–interface interactions but also entropically by excluded volume effects (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the crowding effects.

claim: Protein associations are often enhanced by macromolecular crowding.
source: Consistent with this, protein associations are often enhanced by macromolecular crowding (Minton, 2001), and crowding effects become particularly relevant in a self-assembling structure with multiple units.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Crowding effects become particularly relevant in a self-assembling structure with multiple units.
source: Consistent with this, protein associations are often enhanced by macromolecular crowding (Minton, 2001), and crowding effects become particularly relevant in a self-assembling structure with multiple units.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an explanation for the importance of crowding.

claim: A theoretical study proposed an important role for crowding in the formation of mesoscale assemblies.
source: Accordingly, a recent theoretical study proposed an important role for crowding in the formation of mesoscale assemblies (Marenduzzo et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Macromolecular crowding may have a key role in reorganizing the cytoplasm of starved cells.
source: This suggests that macromolecular crowding may have a key role in reorganizing the cytoplasm of starved cells.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a proposed role for crowding.

claim: The highly ordered structural arrangement of Gln1 into fibrils argues against the possibility that these filaments are protein aggregates consisting of misfolded proteins.
source: This finding and the highly ordered structural arrangement of Gln1 into fibrils argues against the possibility that these filaments are protein aggregates consisting of misfolded proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: Starvation-induced filament formation is not a chaotic protein aggregation event but a desired outcome of a protective cellular program.
source: Thus, we conclude that starvation-induced filament formation is not a chaotic protein aggregation event but a desired outcome of a protective cellular program.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the observations.

claim: During its lifetime, a given yeast cell repeatedly transitions into and out of starvation.
source: During its lifetime, a given yeast cell repeatedly transitions into and out of starvation, suggesting that on evolutionary time scales the yeast cytoplasm must have undergone numerous pH fluctuations.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a consideration about yeast biology.

claim: On evolutionary time scales the yeast cytoplasm must have undergone numerous pH fluctuations.
source: During its lifetime, a given yeast cell repeatedly transitions into and out of starvation, suggesting that on evolutionary time scales the yeast cytoplasm must have undergone numerous pH fluctuations.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an inference about evolutionary history.

claim: Specific adjustments have likely been made to optimize the behavior of protein complexes in an energy-depleted and acidified cytoplasm.
source: This makes it very likely that specific adjustments have been made to optimize the behavior of protein complexes in an energy-depleted and acidified cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a proposed evolutionary adaptation.

claim: Other protein complexes assemble into distinct, starvation-induced structures that do not intermix.
source: This consideration is also supported by the fact that other protein complexes assemble into distinct, starvation-induced structures that do not intermix (Sagot et al., 2006; Laporte et al., 2008; Laporte et al., 2011, 2013; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Assembled Gln1 can no longer undergo the conformational changes that are required for enzymatic activity.
source: How filament formation induces enzymatic inactivation is unclear, but we suspect that assembled Gln1 can no longer undergo the conformational changes that are required for enzymatic activity.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a proposed mechanism for inactivation.

claim: The substrate cannot gain access to the catalytic site in assembled Gln1.
source: It is also conceivable that the substrate cannot gain access to the catalytic site.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an alternative proposed mechanism for inactivation.

claim: When starved yeast cells are re-exposed to nutrients, intracellular pH levels rise and Gln1 filaments disassemble.
source: However, when starved yeast cells are re-exposed to nutrients, intracellular pH levels rise and Gln1 filaments disassemble, thus shifting the enzyme back into its active form.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the experimental observations.

claim: The ability to dissolve filaments specifically affects the ability of yeast to re-grow after starvation.
source: In agreement with this, we found that the ability to dissolve filaments specifically affects the ability of yeast to re-grow after starvation (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 6E.

claim: Preventing the starvation-induced decline in intracellular pH severely impaired the ability of yeast to recover from prolonged starvation.
source: Moreover, preventing the starvation-induced decline in intracellular pH severely impaired the ability of yeast to recover from prolonged starvation (Figure 7A), suggesting that filament formation by metabolic enzymes is required for survival of extensive energy depletion stress.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 7A.

claim: Filaments may be resistant to bulk autophagy, allowing yeast cells to spare vital enzymes from degradation during prolonged starvation.
source: First, filaments may be resistant to bulk autophagy, allowing yeast cells to spare vital enzymes from degradation during prolonged starvation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a possible advantage of filament formation.

claim: Filament formation may promote the transition into or recovery from a more solid and probably protective material state of the cytoplasm.
source: Second, filament formation may promote the transition into or recovery from a more solid and probably protective material state of the cytoplasm, as has been proposed for bacteria (Parry et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a possible advantage of filament formation and supported by a citation.

claim: Filament formation may promote entry into a hypometabolic state that makes energy-depleted cells more resistant to metabolic fluctuations.
source: Third, filament formation may promote entry into a hypometabolic state that makes energy-depleted cells more resistant to metabolic fluctuations (enzyme inactivation by filament formation may provide a buffer against metabolic fluctuations, thus preventing accidental re-entry into the cell cycle).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a possible advantage of filament formation.

claim: Enzyme inactivation may help conserve energy as part of a cell-wide energy conservation program.
source: Fourth, enzyme inactivation may help conserve energy as part of a cell-wide energy conservation program, as has been proposed for mammalian cells containing ADF/cofilin filaments (Bernstein et al., 2006; Bernstein and Bamburg, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a possible advantage of filament formation and supported by citations.

claim: Yeast cells can extensively rearrange the cytoplasm to adjust their metabolism in response to environmental changes.
source: Our findings suggest that yeast cells can extensively rearrange the cytoplasm to adjust their metabolism in response to environmental changes.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the findings.

claim: The cytosolic pH is a key regulator of cytoplasmic rearrangement in response to starvation.
source: We reveal the cytosolic pH as a key regulator of this process and show that assembly into higher order structures can modulate the activity of proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the findings.

claim: Assembly into higher order structures can modulate the activity of proteins.
source: We reveal the cytosolic pH as a key regulator of this process and show that assembly into higher order structures can modulate the activity of proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the findings.

claim: The slime mold Dictyostelium experiences a drop in cytosolic pH during starvation.
source: The slime mold Dictyostelium for example experiences a drop in cytosolic pH during starvation (Gross et al., 1983) and in response to stress (Pintsch et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: pH changes have been shown to control entry into dormancy in bacteria.
source: Among others, pH changes have been shown to control entry into dormancy in bacteria (Setlow and Setlow, 1980), brine shrimp (Busa and Crowe, 1983; Hand et al., 2011), and land snails (Barnhart and Mcmahon, 1988), as well as hibernation in mammalians, amphibians, and reptiles (Malan, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The intracellular pH regulates cellular metabolism more generally in mammalian cells.
source: The intracellular pH also regulates cellular metabolism more generally in mammalian cells (Busa and Nuccitelli, 1984; Moolenaar, 1986), and promotes tumorigenesis (Webb et al., 2011) and the exit from quiescence (Zetterberg and Engstrom, 1981).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Intracellular pH changes are an evolutionarily ancient signal that directs developmental programs and mediates metabolic restructuring during energy limitation.
source: These collective findings reveal intracellular pH changes as an evolutionarily ancient signal that directs developmental programs and mediates metabolic restructuring during energy limitation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the collective evidence.

claim: Gln1 is an essential metabolic enzyme that catalyzes the ATP-dependent synthesis of glutamine from glutamate and ammonium.
source: Gln1 is an essential metabolic enzyme that catalyzes the ATP-dependent synthesis of glutamine from glutamate and ammonium.
evidence: This is stated in the results as background information about Gln1.

claim: The calculated size of a Gln1 decamer is 420 KDa.
source: The calculated size of a Gln1 decamer is 420 KDa.
evidence: This is stated in the figure legend for Figure 2C.
